newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Strikes by S.Korean bus drivers crumble within day.
newsitem.headline: Strikes by S.Korean bus drivers crumble within day.

text.p: Strikes by South Korean bus drivers in Seoul and one other city crumbled in a day on Wednesday, arousing optimism that labour militancy had run out of steam after weeks of stoppages.

Government officials said public bus drivers in Seoul accepted a 5.5 percent wage hike, sharply lower than the 13 percent they had originally demanded. Management accepted a demand for an additional half-month bonus payment per year.
Drivers walked out about 10 hours earlier along with bus workers in two other cities, Taejon and Inchon, stranding tens of thousands of commuters.
The officials said Taejon drivers had accepted a similar pay settlement to end their strike.

The strikes were the first since a new labour law came into force this month, and labour experts said the quick resolution of the disputes augured well for the nation's annual round of weage negotiations.

South Korea was hit by a month of strikes following the passage of an earlier version of the labour law on December 26. The strikes forced President Kim Young-sam to return the bill to parliament for revision.
"Unions have used up a lot of their fighting power in their earlier industrial action," said Bae Sohn-keun, a labour expert at Korea University.
"The bus drivers' action is likely to set a pattern. I'm sure there'll be more strikes in April and May but there won't be a repetition of the disruption we saw in January," Bae said.
The original labour bill, which was railroaded through parliament, allowed companies to lay off workers and banned a militant umbrella union group until 2000.
The law's replacement delayed implementation of the lay-off clause for two years.
It also recognised immediately the formerly outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions that organised the January strikes.
Confederation spokesman Yoon Young-mo said although his group opposed the new labour law it had no immediate plan to stage fresh nationwide protests.
The confederation had asked unions to seek an average 10.6 percent wage rise this year, setting a ceiling of 13.6 percent and a minium demand of 7.6 percent.

"Although we have announced our guidelines, we want to be flexible this year. We believe workers at big conglomerates could accept lower increases as their wage levels are relatively high," Yoon said.

Economists said unions faced an uphill battle to get public support for industrial action as the economy reeled from the collapse this year of two leading steelmakers -- Hanbo Steel Co and Sammi Steel Co.

After the corporate failures and labour strife, the government has revised downward its projection of the country's economic growth to 5.5 percent this year from an original forecast of 6.4 percent. The economy grew 7.1 percent in 1996.

Bus unions in three other cities were originally due to join the strike on Wednesday. But drivers in Pusan, the nation's second largest city, and Taegu reached settlements early in the day and union leaders in Kwangju agreed to continue negotiations.
